profile.reading:
LightEdge Austin II occupies 7000-B Burleson Road, Suite 100, in Austin, Texas, an address that lines up closely with this building's own mapped coordinates near Austin-Bergstrom International Airport. LightEdge's own site names a second, separate Austin location at 2916 Montopolis Drive, Suite 300, several miles away, which this registry treats as the operator's other Austin building rather than this one. LightEdge publishes its Austin capacity and space figures for the market as a whole rather than broken out by individual building, citing 2.5 megawatts of critical IT load and 8.25 megawatts of generator capacity across an isolated 2N uninterruptible power supply design, spread over 58,471 total square feet including 40,960 square feet of technical white space. Because that spec sheet covers both Austin buildings together, this registry does not assign those combined figures to Austin II alone as a building-level number. LightEdge's Austin facilities carry the company's standard compliance certification set, including SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3 audits, ISO 27001, ISO 20000-1, and ISO 22301, HITRUST certification, HIPAA and HITECH readiness, and PCI DSS compliance, with nine on-net network carriers on site including AT&T, Cogent, Lumen, Zayo, and Charter Spectrum.

LightEdge Solutions was founded in 1996 and is headquartered in Des Moines, Iowa, a Midwest data center operator that has grown into a compliance-focused colocation and managed services company with 20 data centers across 12 United States metro markets plus one location in Amsterdam. GI Partners, the private equity and real estate investment firm that also built Digital Realty, took a partnership stake in LightEdge in September 2021. LightEdge changed chief executives effective January 1, 2025, with Jim Masterson, who had led the company for 21 years, handing the role to Rob Carter. Neither LightEdge's corporate site nor its Austin-specific page discloses a year-built date, a tier certification, or a named anchor tenant for either Austin building. Austin has grown into one of Texas's most competitive data center markets over the past decade, drawing large hyperscale campuses from cloud providers alongside mid-market colocation operators like LightEdge, whose business model leans on compliance credentials rather than sheer scale. That positioning is consistent with the company's choice to operate two separate, comparatively modest buildings in the metro instead of consolidating onto one larger campus, giving compliance-sensitive customers a second physically distinct Austin site for disaster recovery planning within the same metro area.

reading.body:
LightEdge Austin II's location within the Austin market cannot be confirmed to a specific address from the operator's own published materials, which list two distinct Austin facilities with an internal discrepancy on one address. The facility contributes to a combined Austin offering of 2.5 megawatts of IT load and 8.25 megawatts of generator capacity across 40,960 square feet of white space, which at a typical colocation density of 5 to 10 kW per rack translates to roughly 250 to 500 racks. No tenant list, year of construction, or Uptime Institute tier rating is disclosed.

The certifications held across the Austin market are compliance-oriented rather than hyperscale-specific: SOC 1, 2, and 3, ISO 27001 and 22301, HITRUST, HIPAA readiness, and PCI DSS qualify the facility to serve regulated enterprise and mid-market workloads. Nine on-net carriers including AT&T, Cogent, and Lumen provide connectivity. This profile is consistent with LightEdge's colocation business model and does not indicate AI training or inference as a primary design intent.

Within Texas, 18 facilities publish power figures totaling 468 megawatts. LightEdge Austin II ranks 19th by capacity, below the published threshold. Texas hosts 133 mapped facilities, meaning the vast majority report no public power specification. LightEdge's decision to operate two separate Austin buildings reflects the metro's growth as a technology hub but this facility's modest power envelope places it outside the tier of campus-scale infrastructure that constrains AI scaling.
